  - some need expensive preprocessing, then break in minutes/seconds
  - originally passive, known plaintext assumption; 2003 more serious: ciphertext-only or active attacker
  - 2006 Elad Barkan, Eli Biham, Nathan Keller: attacks against A5/1, A5/3, even GPRS; tap GSM calls, decrypt real-time or later
- Key length

  - 128 bits then projected secure at least 15 years; now believed secure until quantum computing
  - Audestad, Peter van der Arend, Thomas Haug: British insisted on weaker encryption; Haug told by British delegate it was so British secret service could eavesdrop more easily

  - Golic 1997: solving sets of linear equations, time complexity 240.16 (units: number of solutions of a system of linear equations required)

    - key in one second from two minutes of known plaintext, or several minutes from two seconds; preprocessing 248 steps, ~300 GB of data

  - same year Eli Biham, Orr Dunkelman: total work 239.91 A5/1 clockings given 220.8 bits known plaintext; 32 GB storage after precomputation of 238
  - Ekdahl and Johansson: attack on initialisation procedure, few minutes, two to five minutes of conversation plaintext, no preprocessing

  - 2006 Barkan, Biham, Keller: full version of 2003 paper, attacks against A5/X ciphers
    - [quote: the authors' abstract claim]

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
A number of attacks on A5/1 have been published, and according to internal documents that were released, the American National Security Agency is able to decrypt A5/1 messages routinely.

Some of the attacks need an expensive preprocessing stage, but after that the cipher can be broken in minutes or seconds. At first the weaknesses were passive attacks that used the known plaintext assumption. In 2003 more serious weaknesses were found, which can be exploited in the ciphertext-only scenario or by an active attacker. In 2006 Elad Barkan, Eli Biham and Nathan Keller demonstrated attacks against A5/1, A5/3, or even GPRS, and these allow attackers to tap GSM mobile phone conversations and decrypt them either in real-time or at any later time.

According to professor Jan Arild Audestad, in the standardization process, which started in 1982, A5/1 was originally proposed with a key length of 128 bits. At that time 128 bits was projected to be secure for at least 15 years. It is now believed that 128 bits would actually still be secure until quantum computing arrives. Audestad, Peter van der Arend, and Thomas Haug say that the British insisted on weaker encryption, and Haug says the British delegate told him this was so that the British secret service could eavesdrop more easily. The British proposed a key length of 48 bits, and the West Germans wanted stronger encryption to protect against East German spying, so the compromise was a key length of 54 bits.

### Known-plaintext attacks

The first attack on A5/1 was proposed by Ross Anderson in 1994. The basic idea of Anderson was to guess the complete content of the registers R1 and R2 and about half of the register R3. This way the clocking of all three registers is determined and then the second half of R3 can be computed.

In 1997 Golic presented an attack that is based on solving sets of linear equations. It has a time complexity of 240.16 (the units are in terms of the number of solutions of a system of linear equations that are required).

In 2000, Alex Biryukov, Adi Shamir and David Wagner showed that A5/1 can be cryptanalysed in real time with a time-memory tradeoff attack, which was based on earlier work by Jovan Golic. With one tradeoff an attacker can reconstruct the key in one second from two minutes of known plaintext, or in several minutes from two seconds of known plain text, but first he has to complete an expensive preprocessing stage that needs 248 steps to compute around 300 GB of data. Several tradeoffs are possible between preprocessing, data requirements, attack time and memory complexity.

Also in 2000, Eli Biham and Orr Dunkelman published an attack on A5/1 that has a total work complexity of 239.91 A5/1 clockings given 220.8 bits of known plaintext. The attack needs 32 GB of data storage after a precomputation stage of 238.

Ekdahl and Johansson published an attack on the initialisation procedure that breaks A5/1 in a few minutes with two to five minutes of conversation plaintext. This attack does not need a preprocessing stage. In 2004 Maximov et al. improved this to an attack that requires "less than one minute of computations, and a few seconds of known conversation". Elad Barkan and Eli Biham improved the attack further in 2005.

### Attacks on A5/1 as used in GSM

- 2003 Barkan et al.: active attack, phone pushed to weaker A5/2 briefly, A5/2 easy to break, same key as A5/1; second, ciphertext-only time-memory tradeoff on A5/1 with large precomputation
- 2006 Barkan, Biham, Keller: full version of 2003 paper, attacks on A5/X ciphers; [quote: the authors' abstract claim]
- 2007 Bochum and Kiel: COPACOBANA, FPGA accelerator; first commercially available; A5/1, A5/2, DES; brute force without big precomputed tables
- 2008 The Hackers Choice: ~3 terabyte table; record any GSM call/SMS, key in ~3–5 minutes; tables not released
- A5/1 Cracking Project, 2009 Black Hat, Karsten Nohl and Sascha Krißler; Nvidia GPGPUs, peer-to-peer; from mid-September 2009, equivalent of 12 GeForce GTX 260; any cipher with key up to 64 bits
- December 2009 tables, Chris Paget and Karsten Nohl; rainbow tables, distinguished point chains; parts of 1.7 TB table, three months, 40 CUDA nodes, BitTorrent; ATI Evergreen switch, new format; Frank A. Stevenson breaks
- 2013 Snowden documents: NSA "can process encrypted A5/1"

Several tradeoffs are possible between preprocessing, data requirements, attack time and memory complexity.

Also in 2000, Eli Biham and Orr Dunkelman published an attack on A5/1 that has a total work complexity of 239.91 A5/1 clockings given 220.8 bits of known plaintext. The attack needs 32 GB of data storage after a precomputation stage of 238.

This attack does not need a preprocessing stage. In 2004 Maximov et al. improved this to an attack that requires "less than one minute of computations, and a few seconds of known conversation". Elad Barkan and Eli Biham improved the attack further in 2005.

### Attacks on A5/1 as used in GSM

In 2003, Barkan et al. published several attacks on GSM encryption. The first one is an active attack. GSM phones can be convinced to use the much weaker A5/2 cipher for a short time. A5/2 is easy to break, and the phone uses the same key as it does for the stronger A5/1 algorithm. A second attack on A5/1 is also outlined, which is a ciphertext-only time-memory tradeoff attack and needs a large amount of precomputation.

In 2006, Elad Barkan, Eli Biham and Nathan Keller published the full version of their 2003 paper, with attacks against A5/X ciphers. The authors claim:

> We present a very practical ciphertext-only cryptanalysis of GSM encrypted communication, and various active attacks on the GSM protocols. These attacks can even break into GSM networks that use "unbreakable" ciphers. We first describe a ciphertext-only attack on A5/2 that requires a few dozen milliseconds of encrypted off-the-air cellular conversation and finds the correct key in less than a second on a personal computer. We extend this attack to a (more complex) ciphertext-only attack on A5/1. We then describe new (active) attacks on the protocols of networks that use A5/1, A5/3, or even GPRS. These attacks exploit flaws in the GSM protocols, and they work whenever the mobile phone supports a weak cipher such as A5/2. We emphasize that these attacks are on the protocols, and are thus applicable whenever the cellular phone supports a weak cipher, for example, they are also applicable for attacking A5/3 networks using the cryptanalysis of A5/1. Unlike previous attacks on GSM that require unrealistic information, like long known plaintext periods, our attacks are very practical and do not require any knowledge of the content of the conversation. Furthermore, we describe how to fortify the attacks to withstand reception errors. As a result, our attacks allow attackers to tap conversations and decrypt them either in real-time, or at any later time.

In 2007 the Universities of Bochum and Kiel started a research project to build a massively parallel FPGA-based cryptographic accelerator, COPACOBANA. COPACOBANA was the first commercially available solution that used fast time-memory trade-off techniques that could be used to attack the popular A5/1 and A5/2 algorithms, which are used in GSM voice encryption, and also the Data Encryption Standard (DES). It also makes brute force attacks against GSM possible without the need for large precomputed lookup tables.

In 2008 the group The Hackers Choice started a project to develop a practical attack on A5/1. The attack needs a large look-up table of approximately 3 terabytes to be built. Together with the scanning capabilities that were developed in the sister project, the group expected to be able to record any GSM call or SMS that is encrypted with A5/1, and derive the encryption key within about 3–5 minutes and so listen to the call and read the SMS in clear. But the tables were not released.

A similar effort was the A5/1 Cracking Project, which cryptographers Karsten Nohl and Sascha Krißler announced at the 2009 Black Hat security conference. It made the look-up tables with Nvidia GPGPUs using a peer-to-peer distributed computing architecture. From the middle of September 2009 the project ran the equivalent of 12 Nvidia GeForce GTX 260. The authors say that the approach can be used on any cipher with a key size of up to 64-bits.

In December 2009, Chris Paget and Karsten Nohl announced the A5/1 Cracking Project attack tables for A5/1. The tables use a combination of compression techniques, including rainbow tables and distinguished point chains. These tables were only parts of the 1.7 TB completed table and were computed over three months using 40 distributed CUDA nodes and then published over BitTorrent. More recently the project announced that it was switching to faster ATI Evergreen code, together with a change in the format of the tables, and Frank A. Stevenson announced breaks of A5/1 using the tables generated with ATI.

Documents that Edward Snowden leaked in 2013 state that the NSA "can process encrypted A5/1".

steps.text:
A number of attacks on A5/1 have been published, and according to released internal documents the American National Security Agency is able to routinely decrypt A5/1 messages.[1]

Some attacks require an expensive preprocessing stage, after which the cipher can be broken in minutes or seconds. Originally, the weaknesses were passive attacks using the known plaintext assumption. In 2003, more serious weaknesses were identified that can be exploited in the ciphertext-only scenario, or by an active attacker. In 2006 Elad Barkan, Eli Biham and Nathan Keller demonstrated attacks against A5/1, A5/3, or even GPRS that allow attackers to tap GSM mobile phone conversations and decrypt them either in real-time or at any later time.

According to professor Jan Arild Audestad, at the standardization process, which started in 1982, A5/1 was originally proposed to have a key length of 128 bits. At that time, 128 bits was projected to be secure for at least 15 years, and it is now believed that 128 bits would in fact still be secure until the advent of quantum computing. Audestad, Peter van der Arend, and Thomas Haug say that the British insisted on weaker encryption, with Haug saying he was told by the British delegate that this was to let the British secret service eavesdrop more easily. The British proposed a key length of 48 bits, while the West Germans wanted stronger encryption to protect against East German spying, so the compromise became a key length of 54 bits.[2]

### Known-plaintext attacks

The first attack on A5/1 was proposed by Ross Anderson in 1994. Anderson's basic idea was to guess the complete content of the registers R1 and R2 and about half of the register R3. In this way the clocking of all three registers is determined, and the second half of R3 can be computed.[3]

In 1997, Golic presented an attack based on solving sets of linear equations, which has a time complexity of 240.16 (the units are in terms of the number of solutions of a system of linear equations which are required).

In 2000, Alex Biryukov, Adi Shamir and David Wagner showed that A5/1 can be cryptanalysed in real time using a time-memory tradeoff attack,[4] based on earlier work by Jovan Golic.[5] One tradeoff allows an attacker to reconstruct the key in one second from two minutes of known plaintext, or in several minutes from two seconds of known plain text, but he must first complete an expensive preprocessing stage requiring 248 steps to compute around 300 GB of data. Several tradeoffs between preprocessing, data requirements, attack time and memory complexity are possible.

The same year, Eli Biham and Orr Dunkelman also published an attack on A5/1 with a total work complexity of 239.91 A5/1 clockings given 220.8 bits of known plaintext. The attack requires 32 GB of data storage after a precomputation stage of 238.[6]

Ekdahl and Johansson published an attack on the initialisation procedure which breaks A5/1 in a few minutes using two to five minutes of conversation plaintext.[7] This attack does not require a preprocessing stage. In 2004, Maximov et al. improved this result to an attack requiring "less than one minute of computations, and a few seconds of known conversation". The attack was further improved by Elad Barkan and Eli Biham in 2005.[8]

### Attacks on A5/1 as used in GSM

In 2003, Barkan et al. published several attacks on GSM encryption.[9] The first is an active attack: GSM phones can be convinced to briefly use the much weaker A5/2 cipher. A5/2 can be broken easily, and the phone uses the same key as for the stronger A5/1 algorithm. A second attack on A5/1 is outlined, a ciphertext-only time-memory tradeoff attack which requires a large amount of precomputation.

In 2006, Elad Barkan, Eli Biham and Nathan Keller published the full version of their 2003 paper, with attacks against A5/X ciphers. The authors claim:[10]

> We present a very practical ciphertext-only cryptanalysis of GSM encrypted communication, and various active attacks on the GSM protocols. These attacks can even break into GSM networks that use "unbreakable" ciphers. We first describe a ciphertext-only attack on A5/2 that requires a few dozen milliseconds of encrypted off-the-air cellular conversation and finds the correct key in less than a second on a personal computer. We extend this attack to a (more complex) ciphertext-only attack on A5/1. We then describe new (active) attacks on the protocols of networks that use A5/1, A5/3, or even GPRS. These attacks exploit flaws in the GSM protocols, and they work whenever the mobile phone supports a weak cipher such as A5/2. We emphasize that these attacks are on the protocols, and are thus applicable whenever the cellular phone supports a weak cipher, for example, they are also applicable for attacking A5/3 networks using the cryptanalysis of A5/1. Unlike previous attacks on GSM that require unrealistic information, like long known plaintext periods, our attacks are very practical and do not require any knowledge of the content of the conversation. Furthermore, we describe how to fortify the attacks to withstand reception errors. As a result, our attacks allow attackers to tap conversations and decrypt them either in real-time, or at any later time.

In 2007 the Universities of Bochum and Kiel started a research project to create a massively parallel FPGA-based cryptographic accelerator, COPACOBANA. COPACOBANA was the first commercially available solution[11] using fast time-memory trade-off techniques that could be used to attack the popular A5/1 and A5/2 algorithms, used in GSM voice encryption, as well as the Data Encryption Standard (DES). It also enables brute force attacks against GSM, eliminating the need for large precomputed lookup tables.

In 2008, the group The Hackers Choice launched a project to develop a practical attack on A5/1. The attack requires the construction of a large look-up table of approximately 3 terabytes. Together with the scanning capabilities developed as part of the sister project, the group expected to be able to record any GSM call or SMS encrypted with A5/1 and, within about 3–5 minutes, derive the encryption key and hence listen to the call and read the SMS in clear. However, the tables were not released.[12]

A similar effort, the A5/1 Cracking Project, was announced at the 2009 Black Hat security conference by cryptographers Karsten Nohl and Sascha Krißler. It created the look-up tables using Nvidia GPGPUs via a peer-to-peer distributed computing architecture. Starting in the middle of September 2009, the project ran the equivalent of 12 Nvidia GeForce GTX 260. According to the authors, the approach can be used on any cipher with a key size of up to 64-bits.[13]

In December 2009, the A5/1 Cracking Project attack tables for A5/1 were announced by Chris Paget and Karsten Nohl. The tables use a combination of compression techniques, including rainbow tables and distinguished point chains. These tables constituted only parts of the 1.7 TB completed table, and had been computed over three months using 40 distributed CUDA nodes before being published over BitTorrent.[12,13,14,15] More recently the project has announced a switch to faster ATI Evergreen code, together with a change in the format of the tables, and Frank A. Stevenson announced breaks of A5/1 using the ATI-generated tables.[16]

Documents leaked by Edward Snowden in 2013 state that the NSA "can process encrypted A5/1".[17]
